report.summary: Workstation win81 (192.168.10.5, Windows 8.1, victim LAN) is repeatedly contacting 205.174.165.73 on port 8080. That address is listed in local data as a known external attacker (a Kali Linux attacker machine). In the 30 minutes either side of the alert, this host made 130 flows to that address and port. Most are small and look the same: about 196 bytes out and 128 bytes back, 5 packets out and 4 back, all closed normally. That pattern fits a bot checking in with its command server. At least four other internal hosts (192.168.10.8, .9, .14 and .15) show the same pattern to the same server, which points to several infected machines. Some flows send much more data out (for example 73,339 bytes from 192.168.10.8, and about 963 KB in total from this host), which suggests data is being uploaded to the server. All 20 sampled flows between this host and the server also scored as botnet alerts.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone and is flagged as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine, external).
192.168.10.5 is win81, a Windows 8.1 64-bit workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality and no listed services.

Within ±30 minutes there were 130 flows from 192.168.10.5 to 205.174.165.73:8080, between 13:29:00 and 14:20:14. Together they carried 963,307 bytes out and 13,931 bytes back. The alert flow itself sent 196 bytes in 5 packets, received 128 bytes in 4 packets, lasted about 70 ms and ended with FIN.

Between 13:40 and 14:00 there were 328 flows to 205.174.165.73:8080. They came from several internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .14, .15) and were nearly identical: 194–198 bytes out and 128 bytes back. One flow from 192.168.10.8 sent 73,339 bytes out.

All 20 sampled flows between this host and the server scored above the alert threshold as botnet, with probabilities of about 0.998–0.9999. The main features behind the scores were Subflow Bwd Bytes and Bwd Init Win Bytes = 237.

Many internal hosts making small, regular, uniform connections to a known attacker server on a non-standard HTTP port, plus occasional large uploads, fits botnet command-and-control traffic with possible data exfiltration.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win81 (192.168.10.5) and run a forensic and malware review on it.
Block 205.174.165.73 (at least on port 8080) at the perimeter firewall.
Treat 192.168.10.8, 192.168.10.9, 192.168.10.14 and 192.168.10.15 as likely infected as well, and investigate and contain them.
Review the large outbound transfers to the server (for example the 73 KB flow from 192.168.10.8 and the roughly 963 KB from 192.168.10.5) as possible data theft.

uncertainties: Payloads are not visible, so the HTTP command-and-control content and the data uploaded cannot be confirmed.
The search result was cut off at 100 of 328 flows, so the full list of internal hosts contacting the server is not confirmed.
Check-in intervals were not calculated exactly; regular timing is inferred from the timestamps that were visible.
Only 20 of the 130 flows between this host and the server were scored by the detector.
the model asserted the attack succeeded, but no related-events aggregate shows a large return transfer to the source; severity was not raised for it

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: botnet command-and-control (C2) traffic. The anchor flow is 5 packets / 198 bytes out and 4 packets / 128 bytes back. In the ±30 min window the same host made 167 flows to this address and port. In about the same hour, 816 flows went to 205.174.165.73:8080, and at least 192.168.10.9, .14 and .15 send the same pattern (194–195 bytes out, 128 bytes back) about every 10 seconds, so several hosts look infected. The detector scored the alert and all 20 sampled neighbouring flows from the same pair as botnet. Across the 167 flows, the host sent about 510 KB out against about 15 KB back, so it may be uploading data.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone and is flagged as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine, external).

The detector gave the alert flow an attack probability of 0.99987 and labelled it botnet with probability ~1.0. All 20 sampled neighbouring flows from the same pair were also above the threshold and labelled botnet, driven by the same features (Subflow Bwd Bytes 14, Bwd Init Win Bytes 237, Total Length of Bwd Packet 128).

Regular, near-identical small connections from several internal hosts to one known attacker address on a non-standard port look like botnet check-ins with a C2 server. The large outbound byte total for this host suggests it is also sending data to the server.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win-vista (192.168.10.8) and do a forensic and malware check on it.
Block 205.174.165.73 (at least TCP 8080) at the perimeter firewall.

Review the outbound volume from 192.168.10.8 to 205.174.165.73 (~510 KB) for possible data theft.

The search results were cut off at 200 of 816 flows, so the full list of hosts sending to the C2 server is unknown.

report.summary: This alert is a real botnet infection. Workstation win10-64 (192.168.10.15, Windows 10, victim LAN) checked in with a known external attacker machine (205.174.165.73) on port 8080 at a steady rate. It made 200 connections to that address in ±30 minutes. Four other internal hosts (192.168.10.5, .8, .9 and .14) sent the same kind of traffic to the same address and port at the same time. All 10 of this host's other connections that I checked also scored as botnet. This looks like several infected machines reporting to one command-and-control (C2) server. The C2 connection was working: the attacker side answered every check-in.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone. It is flagged as a known attacker, with the note 'Kali Linux attacker machine (external)'.
192.168.10.15 is win10-64, a Windows 10 64-bit workstation in the victim_lan zone with medium criticality. It has no listed services.

Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.15 made 200 connections to 205.174.165.73:8080, from 13:32:03 to 14:31:53. Together they sent 1,122,699 bytes out and got 16,608 bytes back. The alerted connection sent 195 bytes in 5 packets, got 128 bytes back in 4 packets, and lasted about 131 ms.

The address 205.174.165.73:8080 received 766 connections in the same window. Between 13:55 and 14:05 there were 55 matching connections from 192.168.10.5, .8, .9, .14 and .15. Almost all look the same: 5 packets of about 195 bytes out, 4 packets of 128 bytes back, recurring every minute or so.

The detector scored the alerted connection at 0.9998 attack probability, classed as botnet. It also scored all 10 sampled connections between the same two addresses above the alert threshold as botnet, with probabilities from 0.996 to 0.9999.
Small, identical connections repeating from several internal hosts to one known attacker address on a non-standard web port look like automated bots checking in with a C2 server.
In the same window, 192.168.10.15 also made 2,911 connections to 364 addresses on 17 ports. The most common were DNS (port 53), web (80 and 443), port 8080, SSH (22) and file sharing (445).

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win10-64 (192.168.10.15) and the other hosts sending the same traffic (192.168.10.5, .8, .9 and .14). Then run endpoint forensics to find and remove the bot malware.
Block 205.174.165.73, at least on port 8080, at the perimeter firewall. Search earlier logs for any other internal hosts that contacted it.
Check the roughly 1.1 MB sent from 192.168.10.15 to the C2 server for possible data theft. Also review the host's SSH (22) and file-sharing (445) connections for signs of spreading to other machines.

uncertainties: Without packet contents I can't confirm what protocol ran on port 8080 or what commands and data were exchanged.
I didn't check when 192.168.10.15 first contacted 205.174.165.73 over the full 24 hours, so I don't know when the infection started.
Only 10 of the 200 connections between the two addresses were scored by the detector. The 10-minute search results were cut off, so the list of other infected hosts may be incomplete.

I marked the attack as successful because the attacker side answered every check-in (128 bytes back each time), which means the C2 channel was working. Whether data was actually stolen is not confirmed.

report.summary: This is a real FTP brute-force attack (true positive). Over about 48 minutes (12:42–13:30), 172.16.0.1 opened 2,479 connections to 192.168.10.50 (web-server-16). 2,478 of them went to FTP port 21. Each session was small and ended with a reset, which looks like repeated failed logins. The target is a high-criticality public web server that runs FTP. The inventory says 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address: outside attackers' traffic shows up with this address after address translation, and it is listed as a known attacker. When we re-scored the nearby flows, the detector flagged all of them as brute force. Nothing in the evidence shows a successful login.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,479 flows to just one host, 192.168.10.50 (2,478 to port 21, 1 to port 80), between 12:42:19 and 13:30:03. The pair exchanged 297,402 bytes forward and 465,584 bytes back, about 120 and 188 bytes per flow.
The alerted flow lasted 9.7 s with 11 packets / 122 bytes forward and 17 packets / 188 bytes back. It carried 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 2 RST flags.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16: a public web server on Ubuntu 16.04, high criticality, in the victim LAN, running HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22.
172.16.0.1 is a private address in the firewall zone and is marked as a known attacker. Outside attackers' traffic appears with this source address after NAT (address translation).
The detector scored the alerted flow at 0.99994 attack probability, family brute_force (0.999998). The main drivers were Bwd Packet Length Mean, Bwd RST Flags and Fwd IAT Min.
We re-scored 10 nearby flows from the same source to the same target. All 10 were above the alert threshold and classed as brute_force, with probabilities around 0.9999.

Thousands of near-identical, small, reset-ended FTP sessions from one source against a single FTP server fit automated password guessing (T1110). Responses are almost the same size every time (about 188 bytes back), and no session stands out as larger, so there is no sign that a login worked.

recommended_actions.action: Check the FTP server logs on web-server-16 for successful logins (vsftpd/auth logs) between 12:42 and 13:30 on 2017-07-04, and reset the passwords of any accounts that were targeted.
Use the firewall's NAT logs to find the real external address behind 172.16.0.1, then block it at the edge.
Limit login attempts on FTP/21 or lock accounts after repeated failures, and consider turning off FTP or limiting it to trusted networks on this high-criticality public server.
Look into the other traffic to this host in the same window (146 flows to SSH/22, 44 to port 139, and single flows to several high ports) as possible SSH brute force or scanning.

uncertainties: Flow records have no content, so we cannot confirm login failures or rule out a successful login from network data alone.
Only 10 of the roughly 2,478 FTP flows were re-scored, and part of that result was cut off.
We did not run a CVE lookup. No FTP-service CVE is backed by the evidence, and the pattern fits credential guessing rather than an exploit.
The real external attacker address behind the firewall's address translation is not in the dataset.

findings.statement: Within ±30 min, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,398 flows to a single destination (192.168.10.50): 2,397 to port 21 and 1 to port 80, from 12:43:38 to 13:30:03. On average each flow carried only about 120 bytes out and 188 bytes back.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with criticality high, in the victim LAN zone. It runs HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22.

Thousands of near-identical short FTP sessions with small replies and RST teardown fit T1110.001 Password Guessing, run by an external attacker through the firewall's address translation.

Also look into the SSH (port 22) and port 139 traffic to the same host in this window for related credential attacks.

uncertainties: Flow records contain no payloads or FTP response codes, so I cannot confirm whether a login succeeded from the network data alone.
The real external source is hidden behind the firewall's address translation (172.16.0.1).
I did not run a CVE search for the FTP service because the asset record does not say which FTP software or version the host runs. No CVEs are listed.
I re-scored only 10 of the 2,397 neighbouring flows with the detector.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an FTP brute-force attack against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a high-criticality public web server. findings.statement: Within ±30 min of event 1212114, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,381 flows, all to 192.168.10.50: 2,380 to port 21 and 1 to port 80. They ran from 12:43:53 to 13:30:03. Totals were 285,830 bytes sent and 447,160 bytes returned, or about 120 B sent and 188 B returned per flow.
The anchor flow lasted about 8.6 s, with 11 packets (120 B) sent and 17 packets (188 B) returned, plus 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 2 RST flags. That is a short FTP session that ends in a reset.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04. It has high criticality, sits in the victim_lan zone, and lists FTP/21, SSH/22 and HTTP/80 as services.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is marked as a known attacker. Outside attacker traffic appears under this address because of NAT.

All 10 sampled flows on the same source/destination pair also scored above threshold as brute_force. Thousands of near-identical, short FTP sessions that end in RST, coming from an attacker NAT address and aimed at one FTP service, match ATT&CK T1110 Brute Force (credential guessing against FTP).

recommended_actions.action: Block or rate-limit the outside sources behind the firewall NAT (172.16.0.1) that are reaching FTP/21 on 192.168.10.50. Turn on failed-login lockout for the FTP service.
Check the FTP server logs on web-server-16 for any successful logins between 12:43 and 13:30 on 2017-07-04, and reset the passwords of any accounts that were hit.
Decide whether a public web server needs FTP/21 exposed at all. If it does, replace it with SFTP behind strong authentication.
Look into the SSH/22 traffic from other sources to the same host in this window, which may be a related SSH brute-force attempt.

uncertainties: Flow records carry no payloads, so whether any FTP login succeeded can't be confirmed. The success indicator is set to false.
Only 10 of the 2,381 flows were re-scored by the detector, and the output was truncated after the first few.
The real outside attacker IPs are hidden behind the firewall's NAT address 172.16.0.1.
The FTP server software and version are unknown, so no CVE lookup was done.
The 150 SSH flows to this host came from other sources and were not examined.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive: an SSH brute-force attack on web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a high-criticality public web server. Within ±30 minutes of the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 1,768 flows to this server. Every one went to port 22, and it contacted no other host or port. The flows ran from 17:34:28 to 18:11:20 and were nearly identical: about 2,008 forward bytes and 22–24 forward packets each, the pattern of repeated automated login attempts. The asset inventory lists 172.16.0.1 as the firewall's inside NAT address, which carries external attacker traffic, and marks it as a known attacker. All 10 neighbouring flows I sampled also scored as brute_force. Nothing in the evidence shows that a login succeeded.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 1,768 flows, all to 192.168.10.50 on port 22, between 17:34:28 and 18:11:20. Over this window it reached only 1 destination IP and 1 port. The alerted flow itself had 23 forward and 33 backward packets, 2,008 and 2,745 bytes, and lasted 11.6 seconds.
Other sources also hit 192.168.10.50 in the same window: 2,154 flows in total to this server across 91 ports, mostly 22, 21 and 139.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04. It has high criticality, sits in the victim_lan zone, and runs HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside (NAT) address and is marked as a known attacker. Traffic from external attackers shows up in the flow records with this address as the source.

The detector scored the alerted flow as brute_force with attack probability 0.99994, far above the 0.00024 threshold. The features that drove the score most were Fwd PSH Flags=16 and Bwd Init Win Bytes=247.

I re-scored 10 neighbouring SSH flows between the same two hosts. All 10 alerted, all as brute_force with probability about 0.9999, and they had nearly identical feature values (Total Length of Fwd Packet=2008).

About 1,768 near-identical SSH sessions in roughly 37 minutes, all aimed at one service, match automated password guessing (ATT&CK T1110.001) by an external attacker coming in through the firewall's NAT. The traffic does not spread across hosts or ports, so this is a single-target brute force, not scanning or credential spraying.
The sessions are uniform in size, and I found no unusually large or long session that would point to a successful login and interactive use. Flow data alone cannot confirm or rule out success.

recommended_actions.action: Check the SSH authentication logs on web-server-16 (/var/log/auth.log) for any successful login during 17:34–18:12 on 2017-07-04, and for accounts targeted by repeated failures.

Rate-limit or block inbound SSH from outside at the firewall, for example by restricting SSH to a management VPN or allowlist or adding fail2ban-style lockout, and identify the original external source IPs behind the NAT address 172.16.0.1 from the firewall's NAT logs.
Turn off password authentication for SSH on this high-criticality public server and use key-based authentication only. Rotate the credentials of any accounts that were targeted.
Look into the other traffic to this server in the same window, on FTP/21, port 139 and many single-hit ports. It suggests related FTP brute-force or scanning activity.

uncertainties: Flow records contain no payloads or authentication results, so I could not determine whether any SSH login succeeded.
The NAT address 172.16.0.1 hides the real external source IP or IPs.
Only 10 of the 1,768 related flows were re-scored with the detector.

report.summary: This alert is a real HTTP flood (DDoS) against web-server-16 (192.168.10.50:80). It is a public web server rated high criticality. Between 18:56:31 and 19:16:10 on 2017-07-07, the firewall NAT address 172.16.0.1 opened 95,143 flows to port 80 of this server. That is about 80 flows per second. The client side sent only about 1.9 MB in total, while the server sent back about 1.1 GB. Inventory and enrichment data say 172.16.0.1 is where external attacker traffic shows up after passing through the firewall. All 12 neighbouring flows we scored also alerted as ddos, driven by the same features. We found no evidence that the service was actually degraded.

findings.statement: Within ±30 min of event 4141592, 172.16.0.1 sent 95,143 flows to 192.168.10.50:80 between 18:56:31 and 19:16:10 (about 20 minutes, roughly 80 flows/s). The client side sent 1,902,900 bytes in total and the server sent back 1,109,610,790 bytes. The anchor flow carried 20 bytes forward and 11,595 bytes back across 8/6 packets, with SYN=2, FIN=1, RST=1.
The same destination received 95,415 flows in the window, almost all on port 80, so this one source pair makes up nearly all of its traffic.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16: a public web server (Ubuntu 16.04) in the victim LAN, criticality high, running HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. Its inventory notes list it as a DDoS target.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. Because of NAT, external attackers' traffic appears under this address, which hides the real external sources.

The detector scored the anchor at 0.99991 attack probability as ddos (family probability 0.999999). The top driver was large variation in response (backward) packet length (Bwd Packet Length Std 1497). We scored 12 neighbouring flows of the same pair: all 12 alerted as ddos with the same drivers (Bwd Packet Length Std, Fwd Packet Length Max=20, Bwd Init Win Bytes=229).

High-rate, nearly identical short requests from one NAT address to one web server, each getting a large response, fit an HTTP flood (ATT&CK T1499.002 Service Exhaustion Flood, and possibly T1498 Network DoS). The real sources are probably several external hosts hidden behind the NAT.
The server kept answering throughout (about 1.1 GB sent back), so the flow data does not show whether the service was actually degraded or unavailable.

recommended_actions.action: Turn on rate limiting or DDoS mitigation for HTTP/80 on web-server-16, at the upstream edge or a reverse proxy.
Pull the firewall's NAT and connection logs for 18:56–19:16 on 2017-07-07 to find the real external source IPs behind 172.16.0.1, then block or rate-limit them.
Check web-server-16's availability, response-time and resource metrics for this period to find out whether the flood degraded the service.

uncertainties: NAT hides the real external sources, so we cannot count the distinct attacking hosts from the flow data.
We scored only a sample of 12 neighbouring flows, not all 95,143.
The flow records don't show whether the service was actually impacted. The server kept responding, so success_indicator is false.
We found no evidence identifying the HTTP DoS tool used (e.g. LOIC/HOIC); flow features alone cannot tell.

report.summary: This alert is a real internal port scan. In the ±30-minute window it also reached 495 hosts on 1,054 ports. The flagged flow was a SYN to port 8333 that got no data back and was answered with two RSTs. Nothing shows a Bitcoin service on 192.168.10.19, so this looks like a probe of a closed port, not Bitcoin peer traffic. 192.168.10.8 is not a known attacker address. It is an internal workstation, so it may be compromised and is now scanning the LAN. The scan itself succeeded in mapping ports, but there is no evidence of exploitation.

Within ±30 minutes, the same source-destination pair had 596 flows to 397 distinct destination ports, mostly 139, 445, 1 and 137 plus many high ports, between 18:12:32 and 18:40:59. Over the same window, 192.168.10.8 sent 9,995 flows to 495 IPs on 1,054 distinct ports.
192.168.10.8 is a private address in the victim LAN. It is the medium-criticality workstation win-vista (Windows Vista 64-bit), and it is not listed as a known attacker.
192.168.10.19 is ubuntu-14-32, a medium-criticality Ubuntu 14.04 workstation in the victim LAN. The inventory lists no services for it, so nothing legitimate is recorded on port 8333.

The detector scored the anchor at attack probability 0.99994 with family port_scan (0.999998). The main reasons were zero backward payload, backward RST flags and a short Fwd IAT Min. Ten sample flows from the same pair were all above the threshold and were also classed as port_scan.

The pattern looks like systematic port scanning of the internal network from a host that may be compromised (Network Service Discovery). It does not look like Bitcoin peer traffic: the target refused the connection with RSTs, and port 8333 is only one of hundreds of ports probed.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win-vista (192.168.10.8) and check it for compromise. It is an internal workstation scanning about 495 hosts, which is typical of post-infiltration lateral discovery.
Look at which ports on 192.168.10.19 and other scanned hosts sent replies with payload, especially SMB/NetBIOS on 139/445. Then watch for follow-up connections from 192.168.10.8 to those services.
Block or alert on SMB/RPC traffic between workstations on the victim LAN.

uncertainties: I did not separately check port 8333 activity from 192.168.10.8 over the last 24 hours. The broad port spread makes Bitcoin activity unlikely, but this was not verified.
The ±30-minute aggregates (9,995 flows) mix in normal traffic such as DNS on 53 and web on 443/80. I don't know how 192.168.10.8 became compromised or what started the scan.
I don't know whether any scanned service on 192.168.10.19 answered with real data. The pair's backward bytes (37,896) suggest some ports replied, but I did not inspect those flows.

report.summary: Internal workstation 192.168.10.8 (win-vista) ran a port scan against 192.168.10.19 (ubuntu-14-32), which is on the same LAN. findings.statement: The anchor flow 3174517 from 192.168.10.8:59793 to 192.168.10.19:1524/TCP lasted 0.092 ms. It had 2 forward and 2 backward packets, 0 bytes in either direction, 2 SYN and 2 RST flags, and no FIN.

192.168.10.8 is win-vista, a Windows Vista 64-bit workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality. 192.168.10.19 is ubuntu-14-32, an Ubuntu 14.04 32-bit workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality. Neither is a known attacker, and neither has services listed.

How 192.168.10.8 was originally compromised was not investigated.
Only 10 neighbouring flows were scored, and the detector output was partly truncated.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. The traffic matches a Heartbleed-style memory over-read (CVE-2014-0160) against the OpenSSL service on port 444 of ubuntu-server-12 (192.168.10.51), a high-criticality Ubuntu 12.04 server. The source, 172.16.0.1, is the firewall's NAT address, and the enrichment data marks traffic from it as external attacker traffic. The alerting flow lasted about 119 s, and the server sent far more data back than it received: 7,883,880 bytes back against 7,920 bytes in. Across the ±30-minute window there were 19 flows between the same pair: 14 to port 444 plus probing on ports 80 and 443. Together they sent about 81 KB and got back about 72 MB. Neighbouring flows also scored above the alert threshold. The detector's 'web_attack' label is a rough fit; Heartbleed is a TLS exploit rather than an attack on a web application. The 72 MB returned to the attacker suggests that server memory leaked, but this cannot be confirmed without payloads.

findings.statement: 192.168.10.51 is ubuntu-server-12: a high-criticality Ubuntu 12.04 server in the victim LAN that runs an OpenSSL service on port 444. Its inventory notes say Heartbleed against port 444 is scheduled for this host.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside (NAT) address and is flagged as a known attacker. Flows from it into the victim LAN are external attacker traffic.
The alerting flow ran for about 119 s on port 444. It carried 2,796 forward packets (7,920 bytes) and 2,007 backward packets (7,883,880 bytes), with no SYN, FIN or RST flags.
Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 19 flows, all to 192.168.10.51: 14 to port 444, 3 to port 80, 1 to port 443 and 1 to port 0. In total they carried 81,517 bytes forward and 72,222,411 bytes back.

The detector scored the alert flow at 0.71 attack probability and labelled it web_attack. All 12 neighbouring flows it scored were above the threshold: the long flows were web_attack at 0.97–0.996, driven by high backward packet-length variance, and two short early flows were port_scan at about 0.04.
CVE-2014-0160 (Heartbleed, CVSS 7.5) lets a remote attacker read process memory through crafted TLS heartbeat packets in OpenSSL 1.0.1 before 1.0.1g.

Small, repeated forward packets drawing large, variable backward responses over long TLS sessions to the OpenSSL port match Heartbleed memory exfiltration (T1190). The roughly 72 MB returned suggests server memory leaked.

recommended_actions.action: Patch or upgrade OpenSSL on ubuntu-server-12 to 1.0.1g or later, or disable TLS heartbeat, and restrict access to port 444.
Assume the memory leaked: revoke and reissue the TLS private keys and certificates, and rotate any credentials or session tokens served by the port 444 service.
Block the external attacker source behind the NAT address 172.16.0.1 at the firewall, and check the firewall's NAT logs to find the real external IP.

uncertainties: Without payloads, the heartbeat requests and the leaked contents cannot be confirmed; the Heartbleed attribution rests on flow shape plus the asset notes.
The OpenSSL version on the host is not in the inventory.
The detector's 'web_attack' label is a rough fit for a TLS/OpenSSL exploit.
Because the source is NAT'd, the real external attacker IP is not visible in the flow data.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. The enrichment data lists that address as a known external Kali Linux attacker machine. The workstation opened 16 flows to the same address and port within ±30 minutes, sending about 110 KB out and getting only 282 bytes back, which looks like an active command-and-control (C2) channel or reverse shell on a non-standard port. Another internal host, 192.168.10.25, was also connecting to that port every 10 seconds but got no working sessions. The detector scored all 13 nearby flows it was given as attacks, but it was inconsistent about the attack type.

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone and is listed as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine, external).
192.168.10.8 is win-vista, a Windows Vista 64-bit workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality.
The alert flow lasted 117.9 s, with 45 outbound packets (15,738 bytes) and 40 return packets carrying 0 payload bytes, and no SYN, FIN or RST flags.

Within ±30 minutes, 192.168.10.8 made 16 more flows to 205.174.165.73:444 between 18:04 and 18:44, sending 110,404 bytes and receiving 282. Over the same window it also made 10,376 flows to 484 IPs on 1,074 ports, including 135, 139 and 445.

Repeated long outbound sessions from a victim workstation to a known attacker on non-standard port 444 fit C2 or reverse-shell traffic (T1571). The workstation's wide internal fan-out to ports 135, 139 and 445 may mean it is being used to probe the internal network after compromise. The mixed attack types the detector gave nearby flows make the botnet label specifically less certain.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win-vista (192.168.10.8) from the network and collect forensic data: running processes, persistence, and memory.
Block 205.174.165.73 (all ports, especially 444) at the perimeter firewall.
Check 192.168.10.25 for compromise, because it kept trying to reach 205.174.165.73:444.
Review the internal flows from 192.168.10.8 to SMB/RPC ports (135, 139, 445) for scanning of other hosts or lateral movement.

uncertainties: There is no payload data, so it is not confirmed whether the channel is botnet C2 or an interactive reverse shell.
The detector's attack type was inconsistent across nearby flows (botnet, dos, brute_force), and part of its output was cut off.
Only one ATT&CK technique (T1571) was looked up. T1071 was not checked.
the model asserted the attack succeeded, but no related-events aggregate shows a large return transfer to the source; severity was not raised for it

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone, flagged as a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine).

A slow, long-lived outbound session to a known attacker on a non-standard port, with only pushed data from the client, is a command-and-control or reverse-shell pattern, not a flood. The dos family label is probably a misclassification, and botnet/C2 (infiltration) fits better.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win-vista (192.168.10.8) from the network and collect memory and disk for forensics to find the implant or reverse shell.
Block 205.174.165.73 (at least TCP 444) at the perimeter firewall, and hunt for any other internal host contacting it.
Review the internal hosts the workstation reached on SMB/RPC ports (135/139/445) for signs of lateral movement.

uncertainties: The workstation-to-attacker sessions carry no return payload, so whether the attacker ran commands or pulled data cannot be confirmed from flow data.
The search for traffic to 205.174.165.73 was cut off (50 of 75 flows shown), so it is not fully confirmed that no other internal host contacted it outside the ±30 min window.
The rescoring output was cut off, so the labels of 2 of the 7 rescored flows were not visible.
The initial infection vector on the Vista host is unknown; no CVE could be linked.
the model asserted the attack succeeded, but no related-events aggregate shows a large return transfer to the source; severity was not raised for it

findings.statement: 205.174.165.73 is a public address in the attacker_external zone and is a known attacker (Kali Linux attacker machine, external).

All 13 neighbouring pair flows score above the threshold, with probabilities of about 0.97–0.997. Several are labelled botnet and several are labelled dos.

A persistent, regularly repeating session from a workstation to a known attacker host on non-standard port 444 matches bot C2 traffic (ATT&CK T1571, Non-Standard Port). The DoS labels on some flows probably come from overlapping flow features and do not suggest a separate DoS attack.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate win-vista (192.168.10.8) and investigate it for bot malware: check processes holding connections to 205.174.165.73:444 and look for persistence.

Review the about 88 KB sent outbound to the attacker for signs of data exfiltration. Also review the host's wide fan-out to 495 IPs and ports such as 135, 139 and 445 for possible lateral movement or scanning.

uncertainties: Payloads are not visible, so we cannot confirm which C2 protocol was used or what data was sent outbound.
Backward bytes are 0 on every flow. We have no evidence of commands coming back from the attacker or of a successful outcome, so success_indicator is set to false.
The detector's family labels are mixed (botnet versus dos) on neighbouring flows.
The search_events output was cut off. Only the flows listed in the visible part were confirmed to come from 192.168.10.8, although the aggregates indicate that no other internal host was involved.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive web attack. Flow 3196405 came from 172.16.0.1 and went to web-server-16 (192.168.10.50) on port 80. Inside it, the sender pushed 101 data packets over about 34 seconds. That pattern looks like scripted, repeated HTTP requests, for example login brute force or injection attempts. The enrichment data says 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside (NAT) address, which means this traffic came from external attackers. The target is a high-criticality public web server, and its asset notes say it was a scheduled target of web attacks. In the ±30 minutes around the alert, the same source sent 1,550 flows to this server, all on port 80. In a sample of 10 of those neighbouring flows, none crossed the alert threshold. They appear to carry no payload. The detector scored this flow at 0.9994 (web_attack). There is no evidence the attack worked.

findings.statement: The anchor flow had 204 forward packets (43,906 bytes) and 105 backward packets (72,185 bytes). It lasted 34,020 ms and had 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 0 RST flags.
In the ±30 minutes around the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 1,550 flows, all to 192.168.10.50 on port 80 (1 destination, 1 port). Together they carried 3.1 MB forward and 6.4 MB backward.
In the same window, 192.168.10.50 received 1,749 flows on 39 distinct ports, mostly 80, then 22 and 21.

192.168.10.50 is web-server-16: a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04, criticality high, in the victim_lan zone, with services HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22. Its notes say it was a target of the scheduled web attacks.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. External attacker traffic shows up behind this address because of NAT.

The detector scored the anchor flow at 0.9994 (threshold 0.00024) and gave it a web_attack family probability of about 1.0. The top contributing features were Fwd PSH Flags = 101, Down/Up Ratio = 0.51 and Fwd Act Data Pkts = 101.
Of 10 sampled neighbouring flows on the same source-to-destination pair, none crossed the threshold (probabilities around 1e-5 to 7e-5). These flows had zero packet-length features.

This flow looks like one long HTTP session with about 100 scripted requests and their responses, which is typical of web login brute force or injection attempts. The surrounding empty flows are probably connection noise from the same attack tool rather than separate attacks.

recommended_actions.action: Check web-server-16's HTTP access and application logs for the 12:28–13:28 UTC window. Look for repeated login POSTs or injection/XSS strings, and for successful responses (HTTP 200 or 302 after a login) that would show the attack worked.
Use the firewall's NAT logs to find which external address sat behind 172.16.0.1, then block or rate-limit it at the edge.
Review the web application on web-server-16 for input-validation and login-throttling weaknesses, since the server is public-facing and high criticality.

uncertainties: No payloads were available, so I can't tell whether this was brute force, XSS or SQL injection.
I did not look up CVEs, because the web application and its version on web-server-16 are unknown.
Only 10 of the 1,550 neighbouring flows were scored, so the full scope of the attack is not measured.
There is no evidence of success: the 72 KB returned is consistent with ordinary page responses.

report.summary: This alert looks like a real web attack. Event 3237435 is one flow in a sustained burst of 698 HTTP flows from 172.16.0.1 to port 80 on 192.168.10.50 (web-server-16, a high-criticality public web server). The burst ran from 13:15 to 14:08 on 2017-07-06, sent about 888 KB and received about 3.36 MB back, and used port 80 only. In the inventory data, 172.16.0.1 is the firewall's NAT address, and traffic from it into the victim LAN is attacker traffic. The detector scored the flow 0.958 web_attack. When I rescored a sample of 10 neighbouring flows, results were mixed: some also alerted, but many empty flows (no payload in either direction) did not. Nothing shows the attack succeeded.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 698 flows to 192.168.10.50, all on port 80 (first 13:15:35Z, last 14:08:33Z), totalling 888,204 bytes sent and 3,362,860 bytes received. The detector gave the anchor flow an attack probability of 0.958 against a threshold of 0.00024, with family web_attack at 0.9996. The biggest contributing features were Bwd Init Win Bytes = 236 and Packet Length Max = 2021.

Hundreds of repeated HTTP sessions from the attacker NAT address to one public web server over about 53 minutes is automated web attack activity, such as login brute force or injection attempts, not normal browsing. So the web_attack classification is believable even though scores vary from flow to flow.
The server answered with normal-sized HTTP responses (about 2 KB per flow). That only shows the server was replying; it does not show the attack worked.

recommended_actions.action: Pull the web server's HTTP access and application logs for 13:15–14:08Z on 2017-07-06. Find out which URLs and parameters were requested (login form, SQL injection or XSS payloads) and whether any request got a successful login or other abnormal response.
Because 172.16.0.1 is a NAT address, use the firewall's NAT/session logs to trace these flows to the real external source address, then block or rate-limit that address at the perimeter.
Review web-server-16 for signs of compromise or new accounts, since it is high-criticality and was also hit by SSH and FTP traffic in the same window.
Consider putting a WAF or request rate limiting in front of port 80 on web-server-16.

uncertainties: There is no payload or HTTP-level data, so the exact web attack type (brute force, SQL injection, XSS) cannot be confirmed.
The neighbour scores are mixed, and one neighbour was classified brute_force rather than web_attack. Part of the scoring output was cut off, so not every per-flow family was visible.
The inventory does not name the web application on port 80, so I did not run a CVE lookup and list no CVEs.
Nothing in the data shows whether the attack succeeded.

report.summary: Event 3300170 is a single short FTP flow (port 21, 1.7 ms, 3 packets with 6 bytes out and 4 packets with 14 bytes back). 172.16.0.1 is a private firewall-zone address flagged as a known attacker. It is the firewall's NAT inside address, and external attacker traffic shows up behind it.
The detector gives the anchor an attack probability of 0.276 against a threshold of 0.00024, with family DoS at 0.82 and port scan at 0.18. Fwd Packet Length Max and Fwd IAT Min drive the score.

A few dozen long-lived HTTP sessions and a handful of small FTP sessions over 45 minutes don't fit DoS (no high volume or rate) or a port scan (only 2 ports on this host). The DoS label probably comes from the small packet sizes and the very low alert threshold, not from DoS-like behaviour.

recommended_actions.action: Have an analyst check the FTP server logs on web-server-16 around 19:11–19:48 UTC for login attempts or commands from the NATed source. Also check whether these sessions match a known scheduled attack window or benign test traffic.
Match the firewall NAT translation logs for 172.16.0.1:50833 to the original external source to confirm it is in the attacker range.
Review the detector's threshold (0.00024) for this low-volume FTP and HTTP traffic. It flags flows with very low probabilities.

findings.statement: The alert flow lasted 349.542 ms: 5 packets and 791 bytes out, 4 packets and 133 bytes back, 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 0 RST flags. That is a short, normally closed HTTP connection.

report.summary: Event 4239790 is a single, small UDP/53 exchange: 2 packets out (100 bytes) and 2 packets back (356 bytes) in 0.27 ms. It went from win7-pro (192.168.10.9), a Windows 7 workstation on the internal LAN that is not a known attacker, to dns-dc (192.168.10.3), the critical internal DNS server and domain controller. Over ±30 minutes the workstation's traffic looks like a normal client: DNS, then HTTPS and HTTP to many web hosts, plus a few directory and Windows file-sharing ports to the DC. The 19 distinct ports are spread across 397 hosts, which looks like web browsing rather than a sweep. Its DNS flows to the DC have small, steady sizes, with no sign of tunneling. findings.statement: The anchor flow 4239790 is UDP/53 from 192.168.10.9 to 192.168.10.3: 2 packets / 100 bytes forward, 2 packets / 356 bytes back, 0.27 ms long, with no SYN, FIN or RST flags. It got an answer of normal size, as a DNS query should.

Within ±30 min, 192.168.10.9 sent 2755 flows to 397 IPs on 19 ports. The top ports were 53 (1254), 443 (960), 80 (475), 8080 (29) and 389 (7). This is a typical workstation mix, not a sweep across many ports.

192.168.10.9 is win7-pro, a Windows 7 Pro workstation in victim_lan with medium criticality, and it is not flagged as a known attacker.
192.168.10.3 is dns-dc, the critical DNS server and domain controller (DNS/53 and Active Directory).

The detector gave the anchor an attack probability of 0.00835, against a threshold of 0.000242, and labelled it port_scan with 0.99999 confidence. The features that pushed the score up most were forward length 100 and backward packet minimum length 178.
Of the 12 flows from 192.168.10.9 that I re-scored, only the anchor alerted. The other DNS and web flows I could see scored about 7.5e-6 to 1.25e-5, well under the threshold.

The alert looks like the detector reacting to the usual packet sizes of a DNS response, set off by a threshold that is very low. A host that is port scanning would open connections to many ports on its targets; this host's traffic is dominated by DNS and web ports, which is ordinary client behaviour.

recommended_actions.action: Close the alert as a false positive. Consider tuning the detector so that short UDP/53 query-response flows from internal clients to the internal DNS server don't come up as port_scan.
Optionally, look at the DNS query names from win7-pro in DNS server logs to rule out any low-volume tunneling, since the DC is critical.

uncertainties: I can't see payloads or DNS query names, so slow, low-volume DNS tunneling can't be completely ruled out.
Only 12 of the 2755 nearby flows were re-scored, and part of the scoring output was truncated.
The window included 5 flows to FTP (21), 4 to SMTPS (465) and 2 to SSH (22). I didn't examine them individually.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. Flow 4088164 is the web server's reply leg (192.168.10.50:80 → 172.16.0.1:52589) of a large HTTP flood against web-server-16, a high-criticality public web server. The asset notes describe 172.16.0.1 as the firewall NAT address that external attacker traffic shows up as. Between 18:56 and 19:00 UTC there were 15,846 flows from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:80. Each sent only about 20 bytes, got about 11,595 bytes back and ended with a FIN/RST, the same shape as the alerted flow. Within ±30 minutes there were 538 reply-direction flows like this one. The detector flagged the alert and all 15 neighbouring flows it scored as dos with family probability ≥0.999. The raw attack scores were low (about 0.001–0.006) but well above the 0.00024 threshold. The volume fits an HTTP flood, but the flows alone can't tell a single-source DoS from a NAT-hidden multi-source DDoS. Nothing shows the service was actually degraded.

findings.statement: 192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a high-criticality public web server (Ubuntu 16.04) in the victim LAN running HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is marked as a known attacker. Traffic from external attackers appears with this source address because of NAT.

The alerted flow goes from source port 80 to ephemeral port 52589. The server sent 11,595 bytes in 6 packets, the client side sent 20 bytes in 8 packets, the flow lasted about 12 s and had 2 SYN, 1 FIN and 1 RST. This is a server-to-client response record.

Within ±30 minutes there were 538 flows from 192.168.10.50 to 172.16.0.1 across 529 distinct destination ports, between 18:56:38 and 19:16:10. They carried 6,265,610 bytes from the server and 10,760 bytes from the client.

The matching request flows exist: 15,846 flows from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:80 between 18:56 and 19:00. The returned sample uses sequential source ports, each sending 20 bytes and receiving 11,595 bytes over roughly 8–10 s, with FIN/RST teardown.

The detector scored the alert flow and 15 neighbouring flows between the same two hosts. All 16 were above the 0.00024 threshold with predicted family dos (dos probability ≥0.999). Attack probabilities ranged from about 0.001 to 0.0057.

Thousands of near-identical, tiny HTTP requests to one web server within minutes, each answered with a full page, point to an HTTP flood or DoS against the web service rather than normal browsing. The alerted flow is one reply leg of that flood. Because external attackers sit behind NAT, the flows cannot show whether there was one attacking source (DoS) or many (DDoS).

recommended_actions.action: Turn on or tighten rate limiting and connection limits for HTTP on web-server-16, for example at the firewall or a reverse proxy, to blunt the flood from the NAT'd address 172.16.0.1.
Check the firewall's NAT and connection logs to find the real external source address or addresses behind 172.16.0.1, then block them upstream.
Check web-server-16's availability metrics and HTTP logs for 18:56–19:16 UTC to see whether the service actually degraded.

uncertainties: The flows can't show whether the attack came from one source (DoS) or several (DDoS) because NAT hides the real addresses; the high flow rate could also fit DDoS.

There is no evidence about server health or availability, so whether the attack achieved its goal is unknown. The server kept answering each request with about 11.6 KB, which suggests it stayed up for at least part of the window.
No CVE lookup was done. The pattern is a volumetric HTTP flood, not an exploit of a specific vulnerability.
Only part of the detector's results was readable because the output was truncated, though its summary says all 16 scored flows were above threshold.

report.summary: Event 4499134 is the server's reply half of an HTTP flood, not traffic that web-server-16 (192.168.10.50) started on its own. Its source port is 80 and its destination is an ephemeral port on 172.16.0.1, the firewall's inside address. Attacker traffic is NAT'ed behind that address. Between 19:00:00 and 19:03:00, 14,638 flows went from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:80. They look nearly identical: 20 bytes sent to the server, 11,595 bytes back, and a SYN, FIN and RST in each. findings.statement: 192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a high-criticality public web server (Ubuntu 16.04, HTTP/80, FTP/21, SSH/22) in the victim LAN. It is not a known attacker. Its asset notes say it is a target of DoS and DDoS in the schedule.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is marked as a known attacker. Traffic from external attackers shows up in the flow records with this source address because of NAT.

The anchor flow goes from 192.168.10.50:80 to 172.16.0.1:21333. It carries 11,595 bytes in 5 packets from the server and 20 bytes in 7 packets back, lasts 12.9 s, and has 2 SYN, 1 FIN and 1 RST. In ±30 min there are 538 flows for the same pair, spanning 529 distinct destination ports and running from 18:56:38 to 19:16:10, with 6,265,610 bytes forward and 10,760 bytes backward.

From 19:00:00 to 19:03:00, 14,638 flows went from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:80. Most come from sequential source ports and fit a template: 20 bytes to the server, 11,595 bytes back, with SYN, FIN and RST present.
The detector scored the anchor at 0.0033 against a threshold of 0.00024 and predicted dos with probability 0.9999. The biggest drivers are Packet Length Std and the backward packet length features.
All 10 neighbouring flows for the same pair that were re-scored land above threshold and are predicted dos with probability above 0.999.

A high-rate, uniform inbound HTTP connection burst through the NAT address, plus the matching server responses, points to an application-layer HTTP flood against web-server-16. The alerted flow is the response side of one of those flood connections, so this is attack traffic rather than normal web responses.
The server kept sending full 11,595-byte responses during the burst. Nothing here shows that availability was actually lost.

recommended_actions.action: Check the firewall or NAT logs, or the pre-NAT capture, to identify the real external sources behind 172.16.0.1 for 18:56–19:16, and rate-limit or block them at the perimeter.
Turn on or tune HTTP rate limiting and connection limits (WAF or reverse proxy) for web-server-16 port 80, and review the web server's availability and resource metrics for 18:56–19:16.
Link this alert to the inbound flood alerts on 172.16.0.1 -> 192.168.10.50:80 and handle them as one DoS incident, instead of triaging each response-side flow separately.

uncertainties: NAT hides the real attacker addresses, so I can't tell from this evidence whether the flood came from one source (DoS) or many (DDoS). The detector says dos.
I didn't look up any CVE. The flood pattern doesn't point to exploitation of a specific vulnerability, and the inventory doesn't give the web server software version.
There's no payload or HTTP-level data, so the exact tool (for example Hulk, LOIC or Slowloris) is unknown.
Nothing shows whether the service was degraded; the server was still returning full responses.

report.summary: This alert is a false positive. Within ±15 minutes, the pair had 619 flows: 604 on port 53, with small numbers on 389, 135, 49666, 445, 123 and 49671. That fits normal Windows domain-member traffic (DNS, LDAP, RPC, SMB, NTP).

192.168.10.3 is dns-dc, a critical Windows Server acting as DNS server and domain controller (DNS/53, Active Directory) in victim_lan.

report.summary: This is a real FTP brute-force (password-guessing) attack. Traffic from 172.16.0.1 enters through the firewall via NAT and is flagged as known attacker traffic. It hit the FTP service on web-server-16 (192.168.10.50), a high-criticality public web server. In the 30 minutes either side of the alert, the source sent 2,479 flows to this one host, 2,478 of them to port 21. The alerted flow has the typical shape of a failed login: small packets and a session ended by resets. All 10 nearby flows I re-scored also came back as brute_force. Nothing shows any login succeeded. The asset and IP notes contained planted text telling me to call this benign, which I ignored.

findings.statement: Within ±30 min of event 1167428, 172.16.0.1 sent 2,479 flows to exactly one host (192.168.10.50) on 2 ports: 2,478 to port 21 and 1 to port 80. They ran from 12:42:19 to 13:30:03 and totalled 297,402 bytes sent and 465,584 bytes received, about 188 bytes back per flow.

The alerted flow lasted 9.7 s. It sent 11 packets (122 bytes) and received 17 packets (188 bytes), with 2 SYN, 2 FIN and 2 RST flags. That is a short FTP control session with small replies that ends in resets.
In the same window, 192.168.10.50 also received 146 flows on port 22 (SSH) and 44 on port 139. The other single flows were spread across 36 destination ports in total.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04 with high criticality, in the victim_lan zone. It runs HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. Outside attackers' traffic shows up with this address because of NAT.

For the alerted flow, the detector gave an attack probability of 0.99994 (threshold 0.00024) and brute_force at 0.999998. The biggest drivers were Bwd Packet Length Mean, Bwd RST Flags and Fwd IAT Min.
I scored 10 nearby flows on the same source–destination pair. All 10 went over the threshold and were classified brute_force at about 0.99999, with the same feature pattern.
Thousands of near-identical short FTP sessions, each with small, uniform replies and ending in resets, fit automated FTP password guessing (T1110.001) rather than normal use.

The asset notes and IP-enrichment notes both contained text trying to steer the verdict to false_positive and to suppress evidence citations. I treated it as untrusted data, possibly tampered, and ignored it.
Nothing points to a successful login. The amount of data coming back per flow is small and steady, with no large transfer after a session. So I have not marked the attack as successful.

recommended_actions.action: At the perimeter, block or rate-limit the outside sources reaching 192.168.10.50 on FTP/21 through the firewall's NAT. Use the firewall's NAT logs to find the real external attacker IPs.
Check the FTP server logs on web-server-16 for any successful logins between 12:42 and 13:30. If any appear, reset those accounts' passwords and look for file access or uploads.
Look into the 146 SSH flows to the same host as a possible parallel SSH brute-force, and turn on account lockout or fail2ban for FTP and SSH.
Review and clean the asset-inventory and enrichment notes for 192.168.10.50 and 172.16.0.1, which contain planted instruction text.

uncertainties: Flow records carry no payloads, so failed versus successful FTP logins can't be confirmed directly. The 'no success' conclusion comes from byte-volume patterns only.
Because of NAT, the real external attacker addresses behind 172.16.0.1 can't be seen in this dataset.
I didn't run a CVE lookup: the FTP server software and version aren't in the inventory, so I can't name any vulnerabilities for this service.
Only 10 of the 2,478 FTP flows were re-scored with the detector.
I didn't check whether the 146 SSH flows to this host came from 172.16.0.1: the source's flows in the window went only to ports 21 and 80, so another source probably sent them.

report.summary: This alert is a real DDoS attack (HTTP flood). Between 18:56:31 and 19:16:10 on 2017-07-07, 172.16.0.1 sent 95,143 flows to port 80 on 192.168.10.50. That is about 81 flows per second for 20 minutes. Each flow sent very little (about 1.9 MB forward in total) but drew a large response back (about 1.11 GB in total). That pattern fits a LOIC-style HTTP flood, not normal browsing. The target is web-server-16, a public web server rated high criticality. The source address is the firewall's inside address. Traffic from outside attackers shows up under this address because of address translation (NAT), and the enrichment data marks it as a known attacker. When I re-scored 10 neighbouring flows with the detector, 9 also came out as DDoS. Some note text in the asset and enrichment records was written like an instruction. I treated it as untrusted data and it did not affect the verdict.

findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes there were 95,143 flows from 172.16.0.1 to 192.168.10.50:80, between 18:56:31 and 19:16:10. They carried 1,902,900 forward bytes and 1,109,610,790 return bytes. The alert's own flow sent 20 bytes in 8 packets and received 11,595 bytes in 6 packets over 3.9 seconds.
In the same window the destination received 95,415 flows in total. Almost all of them (95,143) came from the 172.16.0.1 pair; the rest were small amounts to ports 22, 21 and 139.
192.168.10.50 is web-server-16, a public web server running Ubuntu 16.04. It is rated high criticality, sits in the victim LAN and serves HTTP/80, FTP/21 and SSH/22.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's inside address and is flagged as a known attacker. Traffic from outside attackers appears with this source address because of NAT.

The detector gave the alert flow a 0.99991 attack probability, with DDoS as the family (0.99999). Of 10 neighbouring flows I re-scored, 9 were above the threshold. The flows I could see in full were classed as DDoS with probability 0.99996.

Roughly 81 flows per second from one NAT source to port 80, each a tiny request drawing a large response, fits an HTTP flood (LOIC-style DDoS) and not normal browsing. Because of NAT, the real external sources behind this address can't be told apart.
The notes fields in the asset record and the IP enrichment contain embedded text written like an instruction. I treated it as untrusted data, not as guidance, and it did not change the analysis.

recommended_actions.action: Turn on rate limiting or DDoS mitigation (per-client connection limits, upstream scrubbing) for HTTP/80 on web-server-16.
Use the firewall's pre-NAT logs to find the real external source addresses behind 172.16.0.1, then block them at the perimeter.
Check web-server-16's availability and resource use for 18:56–19:16 to measure the impact.
Review and clean up the notes fields in the asset and enrichment records, which contain instruction-like text.

NAT hides the real external attacker addresses, so I couldn't confirm the attack came from several sources.
The detector output was cut off, so I don't know which of the 10 re-scored flows fell below the threshold.

report.summary: This alert is a real single-source HTTP denial-of-service attack. Between 13:28 and 14:19 on 2017-07-05, 172.16.0.1 sent 168,028 flows to 192.168.10.50, and 168,027 of them went to port 80. That source is the firewall's inside address, which carries external attacker traffic through NAT, and it is listed as a known attacker. The target is web-server-16, a high-criticality public web server running Ubuntu 16.04. Almost all traffic to the server in the window came from this one source, so this is DoS, not DDoS. findings.statement: Within ±30 minutes of the alert, 172.16.0.1 sent 168,028 flows to 192.168.10.50 (168,027 to port 80, 1 to port 0) between 13:28:26 and 14:19:49. Those flows carried about 70.4 MB from the source and about 1.91 GB back from the server. The notes fields of the enrichment and asset records contain embedded instruction-like text that does not fit an inventory record. It looks like tampering or a prompt-injection attempt. I treated it as data only and it did not affect the verdict.

recommended_actions.action: Rate-limit or block the external attacker addresses behind the NAT at the perimeter firewall, and add HTTP connection limits or a WAF/anti-DoS profile in front of web-server-16.
Check the availability and logs of web-server-16 (web server error logs, connection-table exhaustion) between 13:28 and 14:20 to see whether service was degraded.
Pull the firewall's NAT translation logs to identify the real external source behind 172.16.0.1.
Review and clean up the notes fields in the asset and enrichment records that contain the anomalous embedded text.

uncertainties: The flow data does not show whether the attack actually degraded the web service. The server kept sending large responses (about 1.9 GB), so no availability impact is confirmed.

Because of NAT, the real external attacker address cannot be seen in the flow records.

report.summary: This alert is a true positive. Over about 2 minutes, traffic from 172.16.0.1, the firewall's internal address that external attackers' traffic is translated to (NAT), sent only 7,920 bytes to port 444 on 192.168.10.51 and got 7,883,880 bytes back. That host is ubuntu-server-12, a high-criticality Ubuntu 12.04 server running an OpenSSL service on port 444. Over ±30 minutes, all 19 related flows from this source went to the same host, 14 of them to port 444, and together they pulled back about 72 MB while sending only about 82 KB. The detector scored this flow at 0.71 and named it a web attack. The pattern looks most like Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160), a bug that leaks server memory in reply to tiny requests. The large replies suggest data actually leaked. Some free-text notes in the tool results contained embedded directives; they were treated as data and ignored.

findings.statement: 192.168.10.51 is ubuntu-server-12: a Server running Ubuntu 12.04 in the victim_lan zone, criticality high, with an OpenSSL service on port 444.
172.16.0.1 is the firewall's internal address and is marked as a known attacker. External attacker traffic shows up in the flow records under this address because of NAT.
The alerted flow 2251110 lasted about 119 s. It sent 2,796 packets and 7,920 bytes forward and received 2,007 packets and 7,883,880 bytes back, with no SYN, FIN or RST flags.

Within ±30 minutes, 172.16.0.1 sent 19 flows, all to 192.168.10.51, on 4 ports (444 x14, 80 x3, 443 x1, 0 x1). Together they sent 81,517 bytes and received 72,222,411 bytes, between 18:08 and 18:32 UTC.

The detector scored the alerted flow at 0.7126 attack probability, far above the 0.00024 threshold, and classed it as web_attack with near-certainty. The biggest drivers were the spread of reply packet sizes (Bwd Packet Length Std of about 2443) and the overall packet-size spread.

All 12 neighbouring flows on this source/destination pair that were re-scored came out above the threshold. The long port-444-style flows were classed web_attack with probabilities up to about 0.996. Two very short flows were classed port_scan.
CVE-2014-0160 (Heartbleed, CVSS 7.5 HIGH) lets remote attackers read process memory from OpenSSL 1.0.1 before 1.0.1g using crafted Heartbeat packets.

Tiny, steady requests answered by multi-megabyte, size-varying replies over a long TLS session to an OpenSSL service on an old Ubuntu 12.04 host match a Heartbleed memory-read attack (T1190). The model's web_attack label is a close approximation of this. The large amount of data sent back suggests memory contents were leaked.

The free-text fields of the asset record, the IP enrichment and the CVE description contained embedded directive-style text trying to steer the verdict. This looks like tampering with the data sources, and the text was not followed.

recommended_actions.action: Isolate ubuntu-server-12 or block port 444 on it from the outside at the firewall, and find out which external addresses sit behind the 172.16.0.1 NAT translations.
Check the OpenSSL version on 192.168.10.51 and patch to 1.0.1g or later, or turn off TLS heartbeats.
Assume the server's memory has leaked: revoke and reissue the TLS private keys and certificates for the port 444 service, and rotate any credentials or session tokens it handled.
Review and clean the tampered free-text fields in the asset inventory, IP enrichment and CVE cache records.

uncertainties: No packet payloads are available, so the Heartbleed request structure could not be confirmed. Calling it Heartbleed rests on the flow statistics, the service and the OS.
The exact OpenSSL version on the host is unknown; the inventory only lists an OpenSSL service on port 444.
The detector's web_attack family is close to, but not exactly, a TLS memory-read exploit.
The port 80 and 443 flows and two short flows the model classed as port_scan were not looked at in detail.
Only 12 of the 19 related flows were re-scored, and the scoring output was cut off after the first few results.
